overall_summary: Space-themed extreme scenarios, particularly 'What If' survival concepts and bizarre planetary weather, are the clear drivers of high engagement and views on FACTVERSE. Conversely, generic psychology facts and repetitive brain-related content consistently underperform. To maximize growth, the channel should pivot towards highly visual, terrifying planetary phenomena and extreme biological comparisons.

winning_patterns.evidence: 'What If You Fell Into the Planet of Burning Ice?' (914 views, 17 likes) and 'What If You Fell Into This $26 Nonillion Diamond Planet?' (490 views, 23 likes) significantly outperformed standard descriptive titles.
winning_patterns.action: Frame space facts as active, dangerous survival scenarios using the 'What If You Fell Into...' hook format.

winning_patterns.evidence: 'The Planet of Burning Ice Will Break Your Brain!' (1,055 views) and 'This Planet Rains Supersonic Rubies!' (721 views) dominated view counts.
winning_patterns.action: Focus on extreme weather concepts (rubies, glass, burning ice) that evoke immediate, strong mental imagery.

weak_patterns.evidence: 'Your Brain Can Create Fake Memories' repeatedly flopped across multiple uploads (5 to 10 views), and 'The Real Reason Songs Get Stuck In Your Head' got only 17 views.
weak_patterns.action: Retire generic cognitive psychology facts and avoid re-uploading identical hooks that fail to gain initial traction.

weak_patterns.evidence: 'The Planet Where It Rains Liquid Metal!' (10 views) and 'This Star Is Older Than the Universe!' (11 views) failed to capture interest compared to more colorful space phenomena.
weak_patterns.action: Avoid purely technical or abstract space data that cannot be easily visualized or dramatized.

next_video.concept: What If You Fell Into the Planet of Supersonic Glass?
next_video.opening_direction: If you stepped onto this beautiful blue planet, you would instantly be sliced into millions of pieces by glass raining sideways at 5,400 miles per hour.
next_video.twist_direction: But the most shocking part? The planet's stunning blue color isn't from oceans—it's the light reflecting off those exact deadly glass shards.
next_video.reason: Leverages the highly successful 'What If You Fell Into...' framing combined with the proven appeal of extreme planetary weather (glass rain) which previously gained solid traction.

experiment: Test a 3-part micro-story series on 'The Most Terrifying Ways to Die in Space' to combine the cinematic space niche with horror/mystery micro-storytelling.
